I am 72 years old and have been farming these flat fields of Quzhou County since I was a boy. I never went to school, but I learned from my father and from watching the crops year after year, and that has been enough. At my age, I do not take risks with new crops or fancy experiments — I stick with the wheat-maize rotation that has fed my family for generations. The winter wheat is already in the ground from last autumn; I sowed it right after the maize came off, using the improved variety from the village supply store. Now that spring is here, I will manage it through to harvest in June, then immediately plant hybrid maize on the same land. I keep about five mu of good irrigated land for this. I will top-dress the wheat with urea and irrigate it three times — green-up, jointing, and grain filling — and spray twice for weeds and insects. For the summer maize, I will have the tractor man come rotary-till the wheat stubble the same day we harvest, plant the hybrid seed, apply basal fertilizer, top-dress at the big trumpet stage, irrigate once, and spray twice. This system is low-risk, the grain buyers come to the village, and at my age I cannot manage the back-breaking labor of vegetables or cotton.
